content: This review is an update of a previously published systematic review on the use of local anaesthetic sympathetic blockade (LASB) for the treatment of complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS). The primary aim was to evaluate the efficacy of LASB in reducing pain and to assess the incidence of adverse effects associated with the procedure. The search for relevant studies included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, as well as conference abstracts and clinical trial registries, up to September 2015. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing LASB to placebo, no treatment, or alternative treatments in children or adults with CRPS were considered. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were used, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. This update included four additional studies, bringing the total to 12 studies with 461 participants. Studies that did not follow up patients for more than 48 hours were excluded. All included studies were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias, and the overall quality of evidence was rated as low to very low due to issues such as methodological limitations, inconsistency, imprecision, and indirectness. Two small studies (32 participants) compared LASB to placebo or sham procedures. These studies did not demonstrate significant short-term benefits of LASB in reducing pain intensity, and the evidence was of moderate quality. One small study (36 participants) with a high risk of bias compared thoracic sympathetic block using corticosteroid and local anaesthetic to subcutaneous injection of the same agents. This study reported significant and clinically meaningful pain reduction at one-year follow-up but not at short-term follow-up. However, the quality of evidence was very low. Two studies investigated the addition of LASB to rehabilitation treatment. Of these, only one study reported pain outcomes, and it found no additional benefit from LASB. The quality of evidence was very low. Eight small RCTs compared LASB to various other active interventions. Most of these studies found no significant differences in pain outcomes between LASB and other active treatments, with the quality of evidence rated as low to very low. One small study compared ultrasound-guided LASB to non-guided LASB and found no clinically meaningful differences in pain outcomes. The evidence was of very low quality. Adverse events were reported in six studies, but all were minor in nature. The authors concluded that the findings of this update are consistent with previous versions of the review. There remains a lack of high-quality evidence to support or refute the use of LASB for CRPS. The limited available data do not suggest that LASB is effective in reducing pain in CRPS, and no firm conclusions can be drawn regarding its efficacy or safety.
